Psychometric tests have become a popular tool in the recruitment processes of many organizations, allowing companies to assess candidates beyond their resumes. For organizations facing similar reliability issues, prioritizing comprehensive test parameters and harnessing user feedback can lead to significant improvements in product integrity. Organizations striving for reliability in their products should consider investing in structured testing protocols like TDD, as well as fostering a culture of collaboration among development teams to harness diverse insights and improve overall quality. Item Response Theory: Enhancing Reliability in Test Development. In the world of assessment and evaluation, the advances in Item Response Theory (IRT) have revolutionized test development, offering exceptional reliability and validity. By focusing on the relationship between an individual's abilities and their performance on various test items, the GRE was able to enhance the precision of its assessments significantly. The Importance of Norming Samples in Psychometric Tests. In the realm of psychometric testing, the importance of norming samples is exemplified by the case of Personality Assessments, Inc. The lesson here for organizations creating psychometric tests is clear: investing time and resources into establishing a robust norming sample not only enhances test validity but also contributes to social equity by recognizing and addressing performance disparities. In conclusion, the reliability of newly developed psychometric tests hinges on several critical factors that collectively shape their effectiveness and credibility. Firstly, meticulous test construction, including the careful selection of items and the use of robust measurement theories, is essential in ensuring that the test assesses what it aims to measure consistently. Additionally, extensive validation processes, such as pilot testing and psychometric evaluations, play a vital role in identifying potential sources of error and confirming the test’s reliability across diverse populations and contexts.

results.title: Validity and Reliability: Key Metrics in Psychometric Test Design and Implementation
results.content: # **Validity and Reliability: Key Metrics in Psychometric Test Design and Implementation**. Challenges in Ensuring Validity and Reliability in Test Development. For organizations looking to enhance their own psychometric evaluations, it is advisable to incorporate feedback loops with data analysis to assess the effectiveness of their measuring tools. Within a year, Unilever reported a remarkable 16% increase in employee retention, attributing the success to the enhanced fit between candidates and job roles derived from reliable psychometric assessments. For companies seeking to implement or improve such assessments, it is crucial to select validated tools that demonstrate high reliability coefficients, typically above 0.7, ensuring that their measurements can be trusted to accurately reflect candidates' abilities and characteristics. By maintaining a thorough validation process and aligning assessments with specific job competencies, companies can ensure that their psychometric testing not only measures reliably but also harnesses valuable insights for fostering talent and driving productivity. In the bustling world of psychological testing and educational assessments, validity serves as the North Star, guiding practitioners in ensuring that their tools measure what they claim to. By actively involving end-users and continuously refining assessment tools, organizations can significantly boost their validity and reliability, paving the way for informed decisions and impactful outcomes. For organizations looking to enhance their hiring processes, integrating well-validated psychometric tests can provide deep insights into potential employees, guiding them toward candidates who align with their corporate values and team dynamics. Challenges in Ensuring Validity and Reliability in Test Development. They implemented a more rigorous validation process that involved multiple pilot tests across various departments, which yielded a final product that not only improved team performance but was also embraced by the nurses themselves, showcasing their input in test development for better alignment. Leaders in various sectors can learn from these experiences: incorporating stakeholder feedback can strengthen validity and reliability, while using diverse assessment methods can mitigate biases and ensure a fair evaluation process. In conclusion, the concepts of validity and reliability are fundamental to the development and implementation of psychometric tests. Validity ensures that a test accurately measures what it is intended to assess, encompassing several types of validation, including content, construct, and criterion-related validity.

results.title: Frontiers | Psychometric properties and validation of the metacognitive self-assessment scale (MSAS) in a Turkish sample
results.content: # Psychometric properties and validation of the metacognitive self-assessment scale (MSAS) in a Turkish sample. (2017) based MSAS scale and the term metacognition in the Metacognitive Multifunctional Model (MMFM) (Semerari et al., 2003) which emphasises common factors underlying constructs such as mental contents and cognitive functions. Discourse analysis, interviews, self-assessment scales, laboratory studies, questionnaires are used to measure metacognition (Pedone et al., 2017; Martiadis et al., 2023). Since there is no measurement tool to assess the metacognition self awareness in Turkey, in this study, the Metacognition Self-Assessment Scale (MSAS) which is a preliminary, quick and simple screening tool for the assessment of metacognition was adopted into Turkish. The Metacognition Self-Assessment Scale (MSAS) is an 18-item self-report instrument developed to comprehensively measure five distinct sub-functions of metacognition, grounded in a functional-focused perspective model known as the Metacognitive Multifunction Model (MMFM). The descriptive statistics and internal consistency reliabilities of the Metacognition Self-Assessment Scale (MSAS) factors were analysed in a sample of 467 participants (see Table 2). In this study, we conducted the Turkish adaptation of the Metacognition Self-Assessment Scale, and assessed the psychometric properties of the measurement tool. In the MSAS score reliability study, internal consistency data were similar to the original, the Portuguese (Faustino et al., 2019) and the Spanish studies (Fernández-Rubio et al., 2023).To investigate the construct validity encompassing the 18 items and four underlying subscales, a first-order Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was undertaken. The findings of the validity and reliability study revealed that the scale has sufficient validity and reliability to measure metacognitive self-evaluation skills. In conclusion, considering the values obtained from the adaptation study of MSAS into Turkish, it can be said that the scale is a valid and reliable measurement tool that can be used in Turkish culture to assess metacognitive self-awareness skills. Establishing future studies that incorporate a clinical sample will improve the scale’s applicability and enhance the strength and applicability of the Turkish version of the Metacognitive Self-Assessment Scale. Citation: Yılmazer E, Hamamcı Z and Türk F (2024) Psychometric properties and validation of the metacognitive self-assessment scale (MSAS) in a Turkish sample.

results.content: Psychometric validation of a culturally adapted health belief model scale for breast cancer screening in Chinese women * Yang Liao,Roles Conceptualization, Data curation, Investigation, Methodology, Software, Validation, Visualization, Writing – original draft Affiliations Department of Community Medicine, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian, Kelantan, Malaysia, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Guiyang, Guizhou, China * Suhaily Mohd Hairon ,Roles Conceptualization, Project administration, Supervision, Writing – review & editing * E-mail:suhailymh@usm.my Affiliation Department of Community Medicine, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian, Kelantan, Malaysia * Najib Majdi Yaacob,Roles Formal analysis, Methodology, Software, Validation, Writing – review & editing Affiliation Biostatistics and Research Methodology Unit, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian, Kelantan, Malaysia * Tengku Alina Tengku Ismail,Roles Supervision, Writing – review & editing Affiliation Department of Community Medicine, School of Medical Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia, Kubang Kerian, Kelantan, Malaysia * Li LuoRoles Resources, Writing – review & editing Affiliation Department of Oncology, Guihang Guiyang Hospital, Guiyang, Guizhou, China Psychometric validation of a culturally adapted health belief model scale for breast cancer screening in Chinese women This study aimed to validate a culturally adapted Health Belief Model (HBM) questionnaire for assessing breast cancer screening beliefs among Chinese women and to evaluate its structural validity and measurement invariance. **Citation:**Liao Y, Mohd Hairon S, Majdi Yaacob N, Alina Tengku Ismail T, Luo L (2025) Psychometric validation of a culturally adapted health belief model scale for breast cancer screening in Chinese women. The three goals of this study are: 1) assess the structural validity of the adapted questionnaire through Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA); 2) examine the cross-cultural relevance and theoretical consistency of the six core Health Belief Model constructs among Chinese women; 3) test measurement invariance (MI) across sociodemographic subgroups, including residential settings and age groups. This diagram illustrates the confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) model of the final 41-item Health Belief Model (HBM) questionnaire for breast cancer screening. ### Structural validity and reliability The final CFA model supported a seven-factor solution that reflected the six theoretical constructs of the HBM, with the self-efficacy dimension empirically splitting into two distinct but conceptually coherent components.
